mcq.passage: In an age of cloud storage and instant backups, it’s tempting to believe our memories—photos, documents, conversations—are safe and permanent. Yet digital memory is surprisingly 36 . Servers can crash, file formats become outdated, and platforms may shut down with little or no notice. Unlike printed photographs or handwritten letters, digital records can 37 silently or be buried in the clutter of poorly organized cloud folders. The overwhelming volume of trivial files creates a kind of digital noise, drowning out what once felt 38 . Even worse, our reliance on technology to remember for us may weaken our own sense of memory and identity. Few people print photos, write journals, or preserve their stories in tangible forms. This shift 39 important cultural questions about what we choose to remember and how we preserve it. Digital preservation is not merely a technical unresolved issue—it is a matter of 40 . Future generations may not inherit photo albums or handwritten notes, but a trail of disappearing data.

mcq.q: Which of the following questions may this passage mainly address?
opts: What are the alternatives to tea bags?
mcq.passage: Tea bags have become a common way to make tea, but there are several reasons why they may not be the best choice. First, many tea bags are made from materials that are not good for the environment. Most traditional tea bags are made from plastic or other synthetic materials. When these bags are thrown away, they do not break down easily and can pollute the environment. This is a big problem in our efforts to reduce waste and protect nature. Another issue with tea bags is the quality of tea inside them. Often, the tea in tea bags is not the best quality. It is usually made from tea dust or small broken leaves, which can lead to a weaker flavor. In contrast, loose-leaf tea tends to have better taste because it is made from whole, high-quality tea leaves. For tea lovers, this difference in taste is important. Moreover, many tea bags contain small amounts of chemicals. To keep the bags in their shape and prevent them from tearing, some companies use chemicals that might not be safe for health, especially when the tea is steeped at high temperatures. The heat can cause the chemicals to break down. This can release small particles into the tea, which we might drink. Over time, these tiny particles can collect in our bodies and possibly cause harm. These chemicals can affect our health and cause problems like hormone changes or other health issues. In conclusion, while tea bags are convenient, they have several drawbacks, such as their impact on the environment, lower tea quality, and potential health risks. For a better tea experience, using loose-leaf tea is often the better option.

The tea in tea bags is understood to be of lesser quality and value.
An ecological process is involved in making tea bags stay in shape.

mcq.q: What is this passage mainly about?
opts: Most rabbits like to eat food with fiber because it tastes delicious.
Fiber is important to the digestive system of rabbits.
Rabbits get sick because they are fed with long fibrous material.
Humans and rabbits share a very similar type of digestive systems.
mcq.passage: Rabbits have three special features of their digestive system that makes feeding the right diet important. Firstly, their teeth grow continuously—an evolutionary adaptation to a coarse or rough fibrous diet found in the wild. In order to keep their teeth from overgrowing, rabbits chew their food in a circular direction—front to back and side to side. This brings all their teeth into wear and keeps them at the right length. This chewing motion is therefore essential for good dental health but only occurs if they spend long periods of time eating long fibrous material like fresh grass and grass hay (this should comprise about 80% of the overall diet). Eating an excessive amount of short-length foodstuffs (such as grain, chaff, and pellets) encourages them to chew up and down like people. The teeth then don’t come into wear and dental disease develops quickly. Secondly, fiber is needed to keep the intestinal tract moving (peristalsis). Low fiber diets can slow, or even stop, this movement. Bloat quickly develops, which is often fatal. Thirdly, rabbits are termed“hindgut fermenters,”meaning that they have a large caecum (a little like our appendix but much, much bigger). Fiber is digested in the caecum (fermentation), releasing nutrients essential to their health. Without high levels of fiber in their diet, this process stops, and the rabbit weakens and dies.
